extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, USPTO disciplinary counsel, and administrative adjudicators handling USPTO practitioner discipline
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural criteria used in USPTO disciplinary proceedings to determine practitioner misconduct and appropriate sanctions (including default judgment rules, specific ethical/regulatory violations under 37 C.F.R., and the four-factor exclusion analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Default judgment for failure to answer (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: "Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in a default judgment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a respondent is properly served and does not timely file an answer, the failure is treated as an admission of the complaint's allegations and the OED Director may move for entry of default judgment; the Court may grant default and deem allegations admitted (as here).

rubrics_metrics.name: Service by publication and answer period (37 C.F.R. § 11.35(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication of the Complaint in the Official Gazette constitutes proper service; the Complaint notifies respondent that he has 30 days to file a response and that a default may be entered if the answer is not timely filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When service by publication is effected, the respondent's deadline to answer is set (30 days here). Proper service by publication supports entry of default if no answer is filed by the deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority/jurisdiction to hear disciplinary proceedings (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.19, 11.39)
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative Law Judges are authorized to hear USPTO disciplinary proceedings pursuant to 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.19 and 11.39 (including interagency arrangements described in the decision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes the tribunal's authority to adjudicate and issue decisions in practitioner discipline matters; cited when determining procedural legitimacy of the proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may not "[E]ngage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance of client funds and then failing to perform the promised services, failing to respond to client inquiries, and keeping the advance without explanation was found to violate this prohibition (court concluded respondent violated §10.23(b)(4)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may not "[E]ngage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to satisfy a court judgment (here, the Harris County Small Claims Court judgment) was found to constitute conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conduct reflecting adversely on fitness to practice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may not "[E]ngage in any other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the [USPTO]."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples applied: failing to deliver promised legal services, failing to return an advance payment, failing to respond to client inquiries, and failing to satisfy a court judgment — all support a finding under §10.23(b)(6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty not to neglect entrusted legal matters (37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not "[N]eglect a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to prepare, file, or prosecute a client's patent application after accepting payment is neglect of a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner; such neglect supports sanctionable misconduct under §10.77(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on prejudicing or damaging a client (37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not intentionally "[P]rejudice or damage a client during the course of a professional relationship...."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to file a client's patent application and not returning an advance payment were found to have prejudiced/damaged the client, constituting a violation of §10.84(a)(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to promptly return client funds (37 C.F.R. § 10.112(c)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall "[P]romptly pay or deliver to the client as requested by a client the funds, securities, or other properties in the possession of the practitioner which the client is entitled to receive."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An advance payment that is not earned by performance (or otherwise properly retained) must be returned; failure to do so (here, not returning $2,000) violates §10.112(c)(4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to keep the USPTO apprised of address changes (agency disciplinary duty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner's failure to timely inform the USPTO of a changed address is itself a violation of the Agency's Disciplinary Rules (as noted by OED).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners are expected to maintain current contact information with the USPTO; failure can affect service and may be independently sanctionable or an aggravating factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction factor 1 — Violation of duty (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b) factor 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the practitioner violate a duty owed to a client, to the public, to the legal system, or to the profession?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts evaluate whether the misconduct breached duties (e.g., failing to perform contracted services, ignoring client inquiries, failing to return funds). A clear breach supports a severe sanction, including exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction factor 2 — State of mind (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b) factor 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the practitioner act intentionally, knowingly, or negligently?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practitioner's intent or knowledge affects sanction severity. In default situations the respondent may waive contesting state of mind, and deliberate, patternistic abandonment supports a maximum sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction factor 3 — Amount of injury (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b) factor 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: What amount of actual or potential injury was caused by the practitioner's misconduct?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider actual financial loss to the client (here $2,000) and potential loss such as failure to secure patent rights (a substantial potential injury). Greater injury supports harsher sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction factor 4 — Aggravating and mitigating circumstances (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b) factor 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there any aggravating or mitigating factors?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggravating factors noted here include: disregard of a court order to repay funds, current suspension from a state bar for nonpayment of dues, total lack of participation in disciplinary proceedings, and patternistic failure to communicate with clients. Such factors can justify exclusion; mitigating factors (if any) would lessen sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy of exclusion from practice before the USPTO (sanction outcome)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court may exclude a practitioner from practice before the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office as a sanction for misconduct after considering the statutory factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After analysis of the four factors and finding violations were knowing and material, the tribunal ordered exclusion (disbarment from practice before the USPTO). This demonstrates the potential sanction for the enumerated violations.
